items.title: Changing Crafts in the Spaces Between States: Formal, Functional, and Decorative Transformations in Fifteenth-Century CE Ceramics at Kirikongo, Burkina Faso
items.who: S. A. Dueppen and D. E. Gallagher
items.note: Documents ceramic change at Kirikongo after its fourteenth-century contraction, one of the West African disruptions later weighed as a possible plague signature.

items.title: Reflections on Plague in African History (14th–19th c.)
items.note: Lead article of a special issue arguing that plague reached West Africa in the fourteenth century, citing site abandonments in the forest zone and breaks in oral tradition.

items.title: Putting Africa on the Black Death Map: Narratives from Genetics and History
items.note: Reads the phylogeny of modern African Y. pestis strains as consistent with medieval introductions and sets out what ancient DNA would need to show.

items.title: Recognizing Plague Epidemics in the Archaeological Record of West Africa
items.who: D. E. Gallagher and S. A. Dueppen
items.note: Cautions that abandonment and contraction cannot by themselves distinguish plague from other causes, and identifies signatures that could.

items.title: Du lexique aux talismans : occurrences de la peste dans la Corne de l'Afrique du XIIIe au XVe siècle
items.note: Identifies Ge'ez epidemic vocabulary, hagiographic episodes and protective texts in medieval Ethiopia that may refer to plague, without fixing the disease.

items.title: A Fistful of Shells: West Africa from the Rise of the Slave Trade to the Age of Revolution
items.note: Synthesis of West African history that treats fourteenth-century epidemic disruption as a plausible but unproven background to Atlantic contact.

items.title: The Black Death may have transformed medieval societies in sub-Saharan Africa
items.note: Reports the case from Ghana, Burkina Faso and Ethiopia alongside sceptics, and notes that early ancient DNA screening of African samples had found no Y. pestis.

items.title: Phylogeography of the second plague pandemic revealed through analysis of historical Yersinia pestis genomes
items.note: Thirty-four ancient genomes from European sites trace second-pandemic diversification, the framework into which any African genome would have to fit.

items.title: The Four Black Deaths
items.note: Reframes the pandemic as thirteenth-century Mongol-era spread from new reservoirs, with one branch of the 'Big Bang' radiation linked to routes toward Africa.

items.title: Témoins africains de crises sanitaires ?
items.who: C. Chapelain de Seréville-Niel and G. Chouin
items.note: Reports ongoing analysis of a 1961 Benin City mass grave of about forty individuals and a child from Ile-Ife excavated in 2019, as candidate plague evidence.

items.title: The source of the Black Death in fourteenth-century central Eurasia
items.note: Genomes from Tian Shan burials of 1338–39 place the second pandemic's ancestral strain there, fixing the starting point for any route to Africa.

items.title: Entwined African and Asian genetic roots of medieval peoples of the Swahili coast
items.note: Human genomes from medieval and early modern Swahili burials; the released data could be screened for pathogen DNA.

items.title: aMeta: an accurate and memory-efficient ancient metagenomic profiling workflow
items.note: Open workflow for detecting and authenticating microbial DNA in ancient shotgun data, applicable to re-screening African sequencing data for Y. pestis.

items.title: Retour sur l’archéologie mortuaire d’époque médiévale dans le sud-ouest du Nigéria
items.who: C. Chapelain de Seréville-Niel, G. Chouin and A. Ogunfolakan
items.note: Examines stratigraphy, body positions and bone markings of the Benin City and Ile-Ife remains against both the plague hypothesis and local mortuary practice.

items.title: Global evolutionary patterns of Yersinia pestis and its spread into Africa
items.note: Genomes of 1,124 modern isolates date the 1.ANT lineage's spread into and within Africa to the late seventeenth century onward, against a medieval introduction.
